Partial application
How partial application in JavaScript fixes some arguments in advance, how it differs from currying, and how to write your own partial function.
Understand how partial application differs from currying, and learn to fix some of a function's arguments in advance to derive new functions from it.
text

Partial application is one of the techniques used in functional programming, in which some of a function's arguments are fixed in advance, producing a new function that waits for the remaining arguments.
Partial application is very similar to currying, but there are differences.
list

Partial application fixes some of the arguments in one step: the result is a function that takes the remaining arguments in a single call and immediately computes the result. A curried function returns a new function after each call until it has received all of its arguments.
The number of arguments passed to the function in partial application can be several, whereas in classic currying it is usually one.

Partial application fixes some of a function's arguments in advance, producing a new function that waits for the remaining arguments.

The function produced by partial application takes the remaining arguments in a single call and immediately computes the result, whereas a curried function returns a new function after each call until it has received all of its arguments.
In partial application several arguments can be passed to the function at once, whereas in classic currying it is usually one.

The partial function from the lesson applies partial application to any regular function: if there are enough arguments, it calls the function right away; otherwise the second call runs it no matter what.

Use partial to fix two arguments of formatMoney(currency, digits, amount) at once — the currency and the number of decimal places — and get toUsd and toBtc. Then get toEur by fixing only the currency: pass it the number of decimal places and the amount in a single call. Print the amounts from the starter.

Compare partial application and currying on volume(length, width, height). Get volumePartial with partial and volumeCurried with curry from Ramda. Print the volume 2 × 3 × 4 computed first with volumePartial and then with volumeCurried: pass 2 in the first call and the remaining arguments the way each function allows. Then print volumePartial(2)(3) and the type of volumeCurried(2)(3), and explain why the results differ.
